answer: itoa_commas writes '-' for a negative value, splits |v| into six decimal digits, skips leading zeros and writes one ',' before the hundreds digit when a higher digit was already written: 1000 -> "1,000", 12345 -> "12,345", 999 -> "999"; an int has at most five digits, so there is only ever one comma. money_format passes it only positive words (florins > 1, groschen, pfennigs > 1), so N0 grouping gives the same text; only -32768 would differ (its negation overflows into garbage characters). It is not assembly only: src/wip/root/text.c has a draft of it.

For a negative number (cur_loc = -1 in world_load and load_game) the DARKLAND.CTY read does start at the file's beginning (the C library's _lseek refuses a negative SEEK_SET offset with EINVAL and does not move), giving the count byte and city 0's first 0x26D bytes, one byte out of place. But the DARKLAND.DSC read of the same load does not start after the first byte: the fgetc has already filled the stream's 512-byte buffer, fflush of a read stream only drops it, and the failed fseek leaves the handle at 512, so city_desc gets bytes 512..591, "y of Mecklenburg" (the end of Wismar's text), NULs and the start of Rostock's (city 0's only if the 512-byte malloc had failed). So nothing in the original treats that record as city 0's; past the end both reads return nothing and the old record and description stay, as noted.

battle_tiles_load copies only the record's size bytes from off into the 'ffx' buffer (one block per used slot 1..15, in slot order) and stores the second frame as a segment, copy segment + ((x4 - off) >> 4), with no bounds check. So a second frame past off+size points into the copies of the following slots in that buffer, or past the end of the 'ffx' allocation. It does not point into the bytes after the record in the decoded .ffc, and the bound that matters is off+size, not the file length. The floor-decoration code picks frame 0 or 1 at random (F_20a5_3474[n*2 + _random_n(2)]), so a stray frame is drawn about half the time. A frame with segment 0 (x4 == 0) draws nothing, because MGRAPHIC's sprite routine skips segment 0.

answer: delay_ticks spins on clock(). MSC clock() returns (ftime.time - t0) * 1000 plus the millitm difference, i.e. milliseconds since start, but it reads _ftime/_dos_gettime, so its value only changes once per BIOS tick (about 55 ms; the game's INT 8 handler still chains to the BIOS every 65536 PIT counts). The 0410:0302 wait counts DS:07D2, which the timer routine 047C:000A increments once per video frame, with the PIT synchronised to vertical retrace. On a 70 Hz VGA display ([07E8] = 4) that routine skips every 7th call, so the 0410 tick is about 1/60 s; the fallback is 0x4DAE PIT counts, 60 Hz.

answer: 1000 ms for 60 ticks is what the code is built for. 047C:000A increments DS:07D2 and is called once per video frame by the INT 8 handler that 047C:0066 installs (the PIT is re-synced to vertical retrace). When the calibration finds a display of about 70 Hz ([07E8] = 4), 000A skips every 7th call (DS:07DA countdown), giving 70 x 6/7 = 60.07 Hz. A display of about 60 Hz ([07E8] = 5), or a failed calibration (fallback 0x4DAE = 19886 PIT counts, 60.0 Hz), also gives 60 Hz. The PAN tick 030B:0508 is called from the same routine after the skip, so it is 1/60 s as well; 86 ms per 6 ticks (70 Hz) would mean the skip was not active in that capture.

answer: The unit is right: clock() is milliseconds since start, and MSC's CLK_TCK is 1000. The duration is not. clock() comes from DOS time (_ftime/_dos_gettime) and jumps by 50 or 60 at each BIOS tick, so delay_ticks(30) (until = clock() + 30) ends at the first change, anywhere from about 0 to 55 ms after the call. With a short loop body, overland_loop therefore runs about once per BIOS tick (about 55 ms, 18.2 passes a second), locked to the BIOS clock.

answer: The Roland driver's only use of the PIT is this calibration. Routine 00CF counts the PIT ticks across a 256-iteration LOOP, and 00FF averages 16 runs (capped at 2600), then stores n x 1024 in [58h] with n = 20800 / count + 1, capped at 63. [58h] is used only as the length of a busy-wait after an MPU reset (0508) and after each SysEx message (04AF), so the emulated CPU speed changes nothing but those delays. With 4 instructions per count the count is about 64, so n hits the cap 63 (64,512 loops), as on any fast real machine.

DS:160C is the citadel court's state, read by the court battlefield builder: the low byte holds the bit of the court door the party comes back through ($LastC11 ORs it from prev_screen: 0x159=1, 0x15C=2, 0x15E=4, 0x15B=8, 0x162=0x10, 0x165=0x20, 0x166=0x40, the court's door order), and when set the party starts at that door's spot with the group count zeroed; the high byte holds the doors of rooms already finished (the trial cards OR 0x101, 0x202, 0x404, 0x808, 0x1010, 0x2020), marked on the court map (cell flags, tile_desc[0x47] = 9). $LastC00 (0x158) reloads it from fact 0x1A tag 1 (created with value 0) with the low byte cleared, and it is saved only in the battle file; so the C#'s BattlefieldContext.CourtProgress ('nothing writes it') is this same DS:160C.
